--- Page 1 ---
eFAIR: Fair LLM Serving under Hourly Electricity
Commitments
You Peng1∗, Youhe Jiang1∗, Chen Wang1, Binhang Yuan1
1HKUST
∗Equal contribution
Abstract
Datacenters can procure electricity in day-ahead markets by committing to energy purchases for
individual hours. For LLM services operating within these hourly budgets, maximizing aggregate
throughput alone may still leave individual requests waiting or receiving much slower service than
desired. Fair serving therefore requires improving service for poorly served requests while reserving
electricity for later arrivals whose timing and demand are unknown. To compare service across
requests, we define normalized throughput as each request’s actual output rate divided by the
product of its standalone throughput and its service entitlement, a positive weight representing its
desired service level. Using this measure, we formulate fair serving as leximin optimization under
an hourly electricity constraint, prioritizing requests with the lowest normalized throughput. To
address this problem, we present eFAIR, an online scheduler that coordinates request dispatching,
electricity budget allocation, and GPU frequency selection through a common normalized-throughput
target. Specifically, request dispatching prioritizes requests by desired service level and progress;
electricity budget allocation reserves electricity for current and expected future work; and fre-
quency selection uses electricity savings to raise GPU frequencies for requests with higher desired
service levels. Evaluations on H20 and H200 configurations, each with 32 replicas, show that
eFAIR improves the tenth percentile of normalized throughput by 28.0%–31.0% over the best budget-
feasible baseline, while keeping absolute deviations from the hourly electricity commitment below
0.26%. eFAIR also improves throughput balance among concurrent requests and aligns electric-
ity allocation more closely with service demand over time. Together, these results demonstrate
how eFAIR improves request-level fairness within an hourly commitment.
1
Introduction
Large language model (LLM) serving must distribute computing capacity among competing requests while
controlling electricity consumption [30, 31]. In this paper, we ask: how can online LLM serving provide fair
request throughput under hourly electricity commitments? This requires deciding both which requests to serve
and when to spend the available electricity. This question involves three key aspects. (i) Online decisions:
The scheduler learns about individual requests only when they arrive and must make service decisions without
knowing future arrivals. (ii) Hourly electricity constraint: An hourly electricity commitment is an amount
of electrical energy fixed before the hour; we treat this amount as an upper bound on the serving pool’s
total consumption during that hour. Hourly procurement in day-ahead markets motivates this accounting
period [4, 9, 27]. (iii) Fair request throughput: Fairness must account for differences in processing cost and
desired service level. We measure a request’s throughput as the number of output tokens generated divided by
the elapsed time from arrival, including waiting and execution. Its standalone throughput, i.e., the average
1
arXiv:2611.24119v1  [cs.DC]  18 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
output rate when served alone under a fixed reference configuration, provides a baseline for comparison. In
this paper, we define service entitlement as a positive weight that scales the desired throughput relative to this
baseline. For requests with the same standalone throughput, an entitlement of 1.5 specifies a desired rate 1.5
times that specified by an entitlement of 1; it does not guarantee that rate. We divide actual throughput by the
product of standalone throughput and entitlement to obtain a normalized throughput score, making service
comparable across requests with different baselines and weights. Subject to the hourly energy budget, our
objective follows leximin fairness [17]: first maximize the lowest score, then the next lowest without reducing
any previously maximized score, and continue in ascending order.
Prioritizing the lowest normalized-throughput scores under an hourly electricity budget is essential because
a system can satisfy its electricity constraint and achieve high aggregate throughput while still providing
poor service to individual requests. A scheduler may process many tokens while leaving some requests
waiting or serving them at rates far below those implied by their entitlements. With a fixed hourly budget,
energy spent on requests already receiving ample service reduces the amount available to improve those
with lower scores. Growing electricity demand from AI services strengthens the need to use available
energy effectively [8, 29]. A request-level fairness objective makes the distribution of that service explicit,
alongside total throughput and consumption.
Two coupled difficulties prevent a straightforward allocation in our scenario. First, requests have different
processing costs and entitlements, so equal compute or energy shares need not produce equal normalized
throughput. Worker assignment, batch composition, and GPU frequency jointly determine both request
progress and energy cost [7, 22]. Prioritizing a request therefore requires execution choices that can translate
priority into a higher service rate. Second, the scheduler must allocate energy across arrival times without
knowing when future requests will arrive. Spending uniformly can restrict service during bursts, whereas
spending only on visible work can exhaust the budget before later arrivals. The scheduler must reserve energy
for running iterations and expected future work, then release savings while they can still improve service.
Existing serving systems are insufficient to address the coupled difficulties of fair service allocation among
concurrent requests and electricity allocation under uncertain future arrivals. For example, vLLM improves
serving throughput through efficient memory management and continuous batching [18]. Virtual Token
Counter (VTC) balances cumulative client service using a configurable cost for processed tokens [30]. EcoInfer
selects GPU frequencies to reduce energy consumption subject to latency objectives [7]. These mechanisms
do not coordinate execution decisions based on individual requests’ normalized throughput with electricity
reservations for later arrivals, leaving fair allocation across requests and time unresolved.
We present eFAIR, an online scheduling heuristic that connects request priorities and electricity reservations
through a common normalized-throughput target.
For concurrent requests, eFAIR coordinates worker
assignment, batching, and GPU frequency according to entitlement and service progress, translating service
priorities into shorter waiting times and faster execution. Across arrival times, eFAIR adapts electricity
allocation to observed demand and consumption, using electricity savings to improve current service while
reserving electricity for expected later work. Our contributions are summarized as follows:
Contribution 1: We formulate fair LLM serving as leximin optimization of normalized throughput under
an hourly electricity constraint (§ 3). We identify three properties of fair serving: effective electricity use,
balanced throughput among concurrent requests, and demand-aware electricity allocation. Together, the
objective and properties connect request fairness to the use of committed electricity.
Contribution 2: We develop eFAIR to coordinate service and electricity allocation (§ 4). REQUEST DISPATCHER
prioritizes requests by entitlement and progress (§ 4.1); ELECTRICITY BUDGET ALLOCATOR maintains shared
reservations (§ 4.2); FREQUENCY SELECTOR uses projected throughput to select execution configurations
(§ 4.3). Together, these components direct the budget toward requests with weaker normalized service.
Contribution 3: We evaluate constrained fairness and all three properties on H20 and H200 configurations
with 32 replicas each (§ 5). eFAIR improves the tenth percentile of normalized throughput by 28.0%–31.0%
over the best budget-feasible baseline, with absolute consumption deviations below 0.26%. eFAIR also im-
proves concurrent throughput balance and reduces the mismatch between demand and electricity consumption.

2
Background and Related Work
We review three areas, starting with LLM systems that schedule requests and control inference costs (§ 2.1).
We then discuss fairness based on resource shares and application performance in networks and training
clusters (§ 2.2). Finally, we review electricity procurement and workload scheduling over time (§ 2.3). This
progression connects request processing, capacity sharing, and electricity consumption.
2.1
LLM Serving Systems
Continuous batching and KV-cache management. LLM serving systems improve GPU utilization by process-
ing multiple requests together. Prefill processes the prompt, while decoding generates output tokens using
the key and value (KV) cache. Orca schedules requests at iteration boundaries, allowing completed requests
to leave and new requests to enter a running batch [36]. vLLM reduces KV-cache fragmentation through
PagedAttention, and Sarathi-Serve uses chunked prefill to limit interference with decoding [1, 18]. These
mechanisms improve serving capacity while controlling batching latency.
Request placement and preemption. Request placement and preemption determine how that capac-
ity translates into response times. DistServe and Splitwise separate prefill and decoding across resources
to accommodate the different requirements of the two phases [23, 37]. Llumnix migrates requests for
load balancing and differentiated service, while FastServe uses iteration-level preemption to reduce re-
quest completion time [32, 35]. These systems manage where and when requests run to improve latency
under shared capacity [11, 13, 14, 24, 25, 33].
Token-based client service accounting. Client service counters guide admission when multiple clients com-
pete for batch capacity. Virtual Token Counter (VTC) measures cumulative client service using a configurable
cost for processed input and output tokens [30]. VTC uses these counters to select requests for admission
to continuous batches and bounds service differences between backlogged clients. The weighted extension
accounts for client entitlements by normalizing each client’s accumulated service by its assigned weight.
GPU provisioning and frequency scaling. Inference systems adjust GPU capacity and operating frequency
to satisfy power and performance requirements. POLCA exploits measured inference power patterns to
support power oversubscription [22]. DynamoLLM adjusts instance count, model parallelism, and GPU
frequency to reduce energy and cost subject to latency objectives [31]. EcoInfer predicts iteration latency
and selects energy-efficient GPU frequencies under latency constraints [7]. These approaches connect serving
configurations to power capacity and energy consumption [26].
2.2
Fair Resource Allocation
Network bandwidth sharing. Network bandwidth is divided among competing flows according to their
service shares. Classical fair queueing and Start-Time Fair Queueing regulate service to backlogged flows, with
weights specifying relative shares [3, 6]. Max-min fairness increases the smallest allocation first, subject to
capacity constraints [10]. Under weighted allocation, service is compared after division by the assigned weight.
The choice of service quantity and weights therefore determines which recipients are considered underserved.
Resource shares and job performance. Cluster allocation extends weighted sharing to multiple resource
types and application-dependent performance. Dominant Resource Fairness compares users by their largest
share of any resource type [5]. For GPU training jobs, Themis introduces finish-time fairness, while Gavel ex-
presses scheduling policies through effective throughput on heterogeneous accelerators [19, 21]. These
approaches distinguish resource shares from application performance, since equal resource shares can
produce different progress rates.
2.3
Datacenter Electricity Management
Hourly electricity procurement. Electricity markets organize purchases and scheduled consumption over
specified periods. PJM’s day-ahead market uses hourly prices, while hourly clean electricity matching aligns
procurement with consumption in corresponding periods [27, 34]. Electrical energy, measured in joules or
kilowatt-hours, is the integral of power over time; a power limit constrains instantaneous power draw in watts.
3


--- Page 4 ---
The distinction determines whether management must limit instantaneous demand or allocate consumption
across a settlement period.
Energy-proportional computing and workload shifting. Datacenter electricity demand depends on hardware
utilization and when flexible workloads execute. Energy-proportional computing seeks to reduce power as
utilization falls, addressing substantial consumption at low load [2]. Carbon-aware computing shifts flexible
workloads using hourly capacity limits while preserving daily processing capacity [28]. Hardware efficiency
determines consumption during and between tasks, while workload scheduling determines when these costs
occur. Both affect the electricity required for a given workload.
3
Problem Formulation
We formulate fair LLM serving as leximin optimization of normalized throughput under a fixed hourly elec-
tricity commitment. § 3.1 first states the constrained scheduling problem and the information available during
online serving. § 3.2 defines normalized throughput, its service target, and the measurement at the hour
endpoint. § 3.3 then uses that target to set the commitment and combines the electricity constraint with the
complete fairness objective. Finally, § 3.4 proposes three properties of desirable solutions.
3.1
Problem Overview
Problem inputs. Online scheduling allocates service under a predetermined hourly electricity commitment as
requests arrive. The problem inputs include the commitment Ch > 0 for hour h, a normalized-throughput
target, and the associated demand estimate; § 3.3 explains how the target and demand estimate determine
the commitment. Resource limits R specify the replica count, memory capacity, and batch limits, while F
denotes the set of available GPU frequencies. Each request reveals a prompt and entitlement at arrival, while
output progress and completion are observed during service. Scheduling decisions therefore use these inputs
and the observed serving history without knowing future arrivals.
Scheduling decisions and objective. The objective is to improve the weakest request service within the
hourly electricity commitment. A scheduling policy π assigns arriving requests to workers and batches and
selects a GPU frequency for each batch. Let Π denote the set of online policies that obey the serving pool’s
resource limits, and Eh(π) the hourly electricity consumption under policy π. We next define request fairness
(§ 3.2), then specify the electricity budget and complete objective (§ 3.3). At a high level, the commitment
constrains feasible allocations, while fairness determines the preferred allocation:
maximize

3.2
Fair LLM Serving
Fair LLM serving normalizes each request’s throughput by the product of its standalone throughput and
entitlement, then prioritizes requests with the lowest normalized throughput. We first define this measure
and its service target, then specify how to compare all requests at the hour endpoint.
Normalized throughput. Normalized throughput accounts for both the effect of contention and the request’s
service entitlement. Let Bi > 0 denote request i’s standalone throughput, the average output rate when
request i is served alone under a fixed reference configuration. Let wi > 0 be the request’s entitlement, Ni the
output token count, and ai, ci the arrival and completion times. For completed requests, actual and normalized
throughput are

3.3
Fair Serving under Electricity Commitments
The hourly commitment bounds the electricity available for fair serving. We use the service target from § 3.2 to
plan the budget, define consumption and commitment deviation, and combine these quantities with hour-end
normalized throughput in the complete optimization problem.
Setting the hourly commitment. The operator sets Ch from the expected workload, entitlement mix, and
normalized-throughput target z from § 3.2. Historical workloads provide an estimate of the requests to
be served; the electricity required to support their target rates zwiBi gives the aggregate service-electricity
estimate bDh. Let ∆h be the hour duration and Pfloor the declared fixed operating power. The commitment
is Ch = Pfloor∆h + bDh. The scheduler receives bDh with Ch to reserve electricity for later arrivals while serving
current work; the appendix specifies the common demand-estimation rule. The commitment fixes the hourly
electricity budget, while scheduling determines when electricity is spent and which requests receive service.
Measuring commitment deviation. Commitment deviation compares total hourly consumption with the
planned budget. Consumption Eh accounts for active execution, idle GPUs, and fixed operating costs. The
signed deviation is δh = Eh−Ch
Ch
and the absolute deviation is dh = |δh|. Positive δh denotes overuse and
negative δh denotes underuse; a policy is feasible in Equation 1 when Eh ≤Ch. This accounting determines
budget feasibility and quantifies how closely consumption matches the commitment.
Leximin objective. Within this budget, leximin fairness improves the weakest observed service first. Given the
hourly electricity commitment Ch, normalized-throughput target z, associated demand estimate bDh, resource
limits R, and frequency set F, let q↑

reducing any previously maximized value, and continues through the sorted vector. Policies with the same
minimum can therefore differ in the service received by the remaining weak requests. This objective defines
the fairness goal; the following properties characterize desirable solutions under the commitment.
3.4
Properties of Fair Serving
We propose three properties for assessing solutions to Equation 3. Effective electricity use concerns the
service obtained from the budget, balanced throughput concerns sharing among concurrent requests, and
demand-aware allocation concerns when electricity is spent. Together, these properties connect the hourly
fairness objective to the allocation decisions made during service.
Property 1: Effective electricity use.
Effective electricity use means improving weak requests’ service
through better scheduling and spending useful remaining budget on further service improvements. The
commitment limits total consumption, so electricity saved by efficient execution creates opportunities to
improve service for requests with low normalized throughput elsewhere in the hour. We assess this property
using the observed frontier between the tenth percentile (P10) of qH
i
and absolute commitment deviation
dh, and report Eh
Ch to distinguish underuse from overuse. A higher P10 at no greater deviation, or a smaller
deviation at no lower P10, represents more effective electricity use among the compared operating points.
Property 2: Balanced throughput among concurrent requests. Balanced throughput means that competing
requests receive comparable service after accounting for standalone throughput and entitlement. Concurrent
requests share serving resources and electricity, so the throughput loss from contention should be shared
according to entitlement. We identify competition by positive overlap of arrival-to-completion or arrival-
to-cutoff intervals, including queueing, and measure rij =
min(qH
i ,qH
j )
max(qH
i ,qH
j ). Larger rij means closer normalized
throughputs: the ratio equals one for equal positive values and zero when only one request produces
output; pairs with two zero values are counted separately. These ratios quantify normalized-throughput
balance among concurrent requests.

Demand-aware allocation assigns more adjustable elec-

more work or higher entitlements. Uniform allocation
can leave busy periods with insufficient electricity while
reserving more electricity than quiet periods need; en-

z. For evaluation, all methods use the same reference
demand profile, determined by request arrivals, work-

TV shows whether expenditure follows service needs across the hour. § 4 develops the online scheduler for
this objective and these properties.

4
Scheduling Framework
eFAIR implements an online scheduling heuristic for the constrained fairness problem in Equation 3. On each
arrival or iteration completion, REQUEST DISPATCHER forms worker–batch assignments (§ 4.1); ELECTRICITY
BUDGET ALLOCATOR determines the electricity available to those batches (§ 4.2); and FREQUENCY SELECTOR
chooses each batch’s GPU frequency (§ 4.3). § 4.4 closes this decision loop with asynchronous execution
and feedback. Figure 3 and Algorithm 1 summarize how the three components turn the hourly budget into
successive service opportunities.

4.1
REQUEST DISPATCHER
REQUEST DISPATCHER controls worker assignment and batch participation to reduce waiting for higher en-
titlement requests while protecting ordinary service and preserving batching efficiency. A batch contains the
prefill and decoding work issued in one serving iteration; unfinished requests continue in later iterations as
arrivals join available capacity.
7


--- Page 8 ---
Prediction and runtime state. Beyond the problem inputs in § 3.1, eFAIR uses output-length estimates
and a profiled execution model to compare candidate actions. The profiled execution model uses offline
GPU measurements to predict iteration duration and power from batch composition, context lengths, and
frequency. For each request that has arrived, a predicted output length b
Ni can be supplied by a prompt-based
predictor [16]. The profiled execution model then estimates standalone throughput bBi for that length;
Appendix C describes the profiles and calibration checks. eFAIR maintains observed output ni(t), elapsed
waiting time, queue assignments, worker availability, and electricity reservations. These estimates support
comparisons of normalized throughput and electricity cost.
Normalized throughput during serving. REQUEST DISPATCHER tracks normalized throughput to compare
service progress while requests remain active. At t > ai, the online estimate is bqi(t) =
ni(t)
wi b
Bi(t−ai), whose
denominator includes queueing, prefill, and decoding. After output begins, waiting without output lowers
normalized throughput, while execution advances the numerator. Before output begins, observed throughput
is zero, so eFAIR predicts completion throughput from elapsed waiting, predicted length, and estimated
standalone throughput. Both cases include time already spent waiting when determining request priority.
Worker assignment. REQUEST DISPATCHER consolidates ordinary requests (wi = 1) and gives admission
preference to higher entitlement requests (wi > 1). For higher entitlement arrivals, eFAIR prefers idle workers,
then favors workers whose residents have the same entitlement, considering capacity and congestion. A worker
serving only ordinary requests can accept the arriving request when its resident requests can yield the next batch
under the priority rule below and the new request can be admitted no later than it would be on the preferred
worker. For ordinary arrivals, eFAIR favors batches of ordinary requests but uses an idle worker when either
a resident request’s normalized throughput or the arriving request’s predicted normalized throughput after
waiting for admission falls below the median for active requests with higher entitlements that have produced
output. These rules combine earlier admission for higher entitlements with efficient batching of ordinary work.
Batch priority. REQUEST DISPATCHER gives higher entitlement requests priority when ordinary requests’ nor-
malized throughput is sufficiently high. On a shared worker, every ordinary resident’s normalized throughput
must reach both z and the median normalized throughput of active higher entitlement requests that have
produced output. If this median is unavailable, the threshold is z; ordinary requests without output use
their predicted normalized throughput at completion. When the condition holds, higher entitlement requests
receive priority for the next batch; otherwise, both classes remain eligible. Batches obey token, sequence,
and KV-memory limits, yielding ready worker–batch pairs P. These rules give higher entitlement requests
additional service opportunities while retaining ordinary access to shared capacity; the resulting ready batches
receive electricity allocations in § 4.2.
4.2
ELECTRICITY BUDGET ALLOCATOR
ELECTRICITY BUDGET ALLOCATOR translates the hourly commitment into a shared budget for current work by
accounting for past consumption, running iterations’ reserved electricity, and expected later demand.
Electricity reservations. The account deducts past consumption, future fixed costs, and electricity reserved
for running work before allocating new service. At time t in hour h, let Eh(t) denote realized consumption,
Pfloor the declared fixed operating power, H the hour endpoint, and bErun(t) the incremental electricity still
owed to running work. The electricity remaining for uncommitted service is
Rh(t) = Ch −Eh(t) −Pfloor(H −t) −bErun(t).
(5)
Completion feedback reconciles reservations with consumption, preventing duplicate allocations across
workers.
Current and future demand. ELECTRICITY BUDGET ALLOCATOR divides the remaining electricity between
arrived work and later arrivals. For arrived work, eFAIR estimates remaining demand using z, entitlements, pre-
dicted lengths, and observed output. For later arrivals, eFAIR uses the aggregate estimate associated with Ch,
accounting for requests already observed. Reserving a proportional share of Rh(t) for later arrivals leaves the
8


--- Page 9 ---
current shared budget A(t). All current batches draw from this budget, with reserved work excluded from un-
committed demand. Each launch reserves electricity before the next allocation, so batches share one account.
Surplus electricity. The shared surplus S(t) is the nonnegative electricity left after covering current and future
service demand at target z. At a higher GPU frequency, the predicted incremental electricity consumption
of the next iteration must not exceed the current budget A(t), and the additional electricity required for
acceleration must not exceed the shared surplus S(t). These two checks permit acceleration while preserving
the shared allocation; the appendix gives the budget formulas. § 4.3 uses the shared budget and surplus to
select GPU frequencies for each ready worker–batch pair.
4.3
FREQUENCY SELECTOR
For each batch, FREQUENCY SELECTOR uses projected service and electricity cost to select a frequency for the
common target, then considers additional acceleration for work with higher entitlements.
Throughput and electricity prediction. The profiled execution model introduced in § 4.1 estimates execution
costs at each candidate frequency. For batch B and f ∈F, the model estimates iteration duration bτ(B, f) and
incremental electricity bE(B, f). The output-length estimate b
Ni and observed progress turn these execution
estimates into average throughput bTi(f) through completion or the hour endpoint, including elapsed waiting
and output already produced. Predicted normalized throughput is bqi(f) =
b
Ti(f)
wi b
Bi . Decode-only predictions use
batch speed and context costs; supported prefill predictions include remaining prefill and decoding, linking
each candidate frequency to the request’s projected service.
Meeting the service target. FREQUENCY SELECTOR chooses the least costly affordable frequency predicted
to meet the target for all batch members. Affordability requires bE(B, f) ≤A(t); target feasibility requires a
valid completion prediction with mini∈B bqi(f) ≥z. eFAIR compares next-iteration electricity for decode-only
batches and predicted remaining service electricity for prefill batches of ordinary requests when that estimate
is available. The chosen frequency minimizes the applicable cost estimate; each launch reserves only the
electricity needed for the next iteration.
Fallback frequency selection. FREQUENCY SELECTOR favors fast execution when no frequency can meet the tar-
get or completion predictions are unavailable. eFAIR selects the frequency with the shortest predicted iteration
time among those whose electricity fits A(t). If none fits, eFAIR minimizes predicted iteration electricity and
records the expenditure. One-iteration decisions let subsequent choices use updated progress and consumption.
Acceleration with surplus electricity. After reserving electricity for current and future service demand at
target z (§ 4.2), FREQUENCY SELECTOR uses the surplus S(t) to accelerate higher entitlement batches. Relative
to the selected frequency f0, a faster frequency must keep predicted iteration electricity within A(t) and spend
at most S(t) more. If f0 meets the target, acceleration must preserve the target for every batch member. If
no faster frequency qualifies, eFAIR retains f0. Savings from batching and frequency selection thus support
faster service for higher entitlement requests. Execution feedback then updates the estimates and reservations
used by the next decision (§ 4.4).
4.4
Asynchronous Execution
Execution feedback keeps service predictions and electricity reservations aligned with current progress. The
scheduler asynchronously prepares subsequent batches while already launched GPU work continues. Arrivals
and iteration completions update request progress, worker availability, and electricity reservations before
triggering the next decision. When an unfinished request reaches its predicted output length, its length estimate
is extended; when it completes, its electricity-demand estimate is reconciled using the final output-token count.
§ 5.4 evaluates sensitivity to length errors. At iteration boundaries, workers admit arrivals, continue unfinished
requests, and remove completed requests within capacity limits. Each launch reserves electricity before another
allocation, and scheduler response time affects subsequent launches. These updates let subsequent decisions
incorporate observed progress and consumption while preserving asynchronous execution.
9


--- Page 10 ---
5
Evaluation
We evaluate whether eFAIR improves fair LLM serving under hourly electricity commitments through three
questions. After describing the experimental setup (§ 5.1), we evaluate the constrained fairness objective
(§ 5.2), assess the three properties of fair serving (§ 5.3), and examine scheduling efficiency and robustness
(§ 5.4).
• RQ1: How does eFAIR improve the fairness objective while satisfying the hourly electricity commitment?
• RQ2: How well does eFAIR achieve the following properties: effective electricity use, balanced throughput
among concurrent requests, and demand-aware electricity allocation? (Properties 1–3, § 3.4.)
• RQ3: How quickly does eFAIR make online scheduling decisions, and how robust is the resulting service
to output-length prediction errors?
5.1
Experimental Setup
Methods share the same requests and hourly commitments. We measure service using normalized throughput
qH
i (§ 3.2): output produced by the hour’s end divided by elapsed request time, standalone throughput (the
output rate when served alone), and entitlement. Elapsed time runs from arrival to completion, or to the hour
boundary for unfinished requests; larger qH
i indicates better normalized service.
Runtime configuration. We evaluate Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 with tensor parallelism of one (TP=1) in H20 and
H200 configurations, each with 32 model replicas.
Workload traces. The H20 configuration replays the Azure inference trace from May 12, 2024, 14:00 to
15:00 UTC (35,597 requests); H200 uses a heavier trace from May 11, 2024, 00:00 to 01:00 UTC (60,686
requests) [20]. Both use entitlements wi ∈{1, 1.5}. The main comparison supplies true recorded output
lengths ( b
Ni = Ni) and an accurate estimate of the total service-electricity demand used to set Ch. § 5.4
evaluates errors in the per-request output-length estimates.
Hourly commitments. All methods use the same electricity budget for each workload. We set the normalized-
throughput target z = 0.6 before evaluating the policies, estimate the electricity needed for the request mix
and entitlements, and add the pool’s fixed operating cost. The commitments are 17.68 MJ for H20 and
19.01 MJ for H200. A configuration satisfies the commitment when its realized consumption obeys Eh ≤Ch.
Baselines. We compare methods that prioritize aggregate throughput, client fairness, or electricity efficiency.
• vLLM uses continuous batching and KV-cache management for efficient serving [18].
• Weighted VTC prioritizes clients according to accumulated service relative to their entitlements [30]. We
use costs derived from profiling to account for each client’s accumulated service.
• EcoInfer selects iteration frequencies to reduce electricity use while meeting its latency objective [7]. We
retain that objective in the comparison.
vLLM and Weighted VTC do not account for hourly electricity commitments and exceed the budget at their
default frequencies. For RQ1, we retain their scheduling policies and select frequencies whose consumption
is closest to the commitment without exceeding the commitment: 1365 MHz on H20 and 1170 MHz on
H200. The effective-electricity comparison in RQ2 also includes their default frequencies; all other baseline
comparisons use configurations that satisfy the commitment.
Evaluation metrics. RQ1 compares the leximin objective and the distribution of normalized throughput.
Leximin sorts qH
i
from lowest to highest and compares methods at the first rank where the values differ
(Equation 3). We report the minimum Qmin, zero-output counts, P10, and P1, where P10 and P1 are the tenth
and first percentiles of qH
i . Each request has equal weight; a higher value at a given percentile indicates better
normalized service. RQ2 assesses P10 against absolute commitment deviation dh (§ 3.3), concurrent-request
throughput ratios rij (Property 2 in § 3.4), and temporal demand–electricity mismatch measured by total
variation (TV; Equation 4). RQ3 measures scheduling response time and changes in request-level P10 under
output-length errors. Each property result explains the corresponding metric.
10


--- Page 11 ---
5.2
Fairness within the Hourly Commitment
Leximin fairness. eFAIR improves the objective in Equation 3 over all baseline configurations satisfying the
hourly commitment, answering RQ1 (Table 1). All methods have the same minimum normalized throughput
of zero because some requests arriving within the final 1.24 s on H20 or 0.96 s on H200 produce no output
before the hour ends. eFAIR leaves six and four such requests, respectively, versus at least seven and five for
the baselines. At the first differing rank, 7 on H20 and 5 on H200, eFAIR achieves normalized throughput
of 0.1544 and 0.0158, while every baseline still has zero. The sorted eFAIR normalized-throughput vector
therefore ranks above each baseline under the leximin objective.

Service improvements for weak requests. eFAIR’s
leximin advantage is accompanied by higher lower-

197.0% over the baselines that satisfy the commit-
ment. On H20, P10 increases by 31.7% over vLLM
and 31.0% over Weighted VTC, with electricity dif-
fering by less than 0.04%. On H200, the gains are
29.3% and 28.0%, using 3.1% to 3.2% more elec-
tricity within the commitment. The P10 gains over
EcoInfer are 100.1% and 197.0%, respectively. P1
also increases to 0.4649 on H20 and 0.4339 on H200,
compared with baseline ranges of 0.1898–0.3229 and

tration of requests at higher normalized throughput
under eFAIR. To determine whether requests poorly served by the baselines benefit, we select the 10% of
requests with the lowest qH
i
under each baseline and compare those same requests under eFAIR. Across
these groups, eFAIR improves 3,522–3,549 of 3,560 requests on H20 and 5,989–6,043 of 6,069 on H200;
detailed counts appear in the supplementary appendix. Together, the percentile gains and comparisons of
the same requests show that the improvement extends beyond the first differing rank and reaches requests
with the weakest baseline service.
Explaining baseline performance. The results are consistent with differences in how the methods allocate
service and control GPU frequency. vLLM favors efficient batching without explicitly prioritizing requests with
low normalized throughput. Weighted VTC changes batch-admission order to balance accumulated client
service relative to entitlement; when client service is already balanced, this ordering offers limited scope to
improve individual request throughput. The evaluated vLLM and Weighted VTC configurations also use the
same fixed GPU frequency, consistent with their similar P10. EcoInfer selects energy-saving frequencies to
meet latency requirements, without explicitly using the remaining hourly budget to improve requests with
low normalized throughput. eFAIR coordinates batch participation and GPU frequency selection to direct the
available electricity toward these requests.

Balanced throughput among concurrent requests. eFAIR improves normalized-throughput balance among
requests that compete for service. For Property 2, rij is the smaller of two concurrent requests’ normalized
throughputs divided by the larger; a ratio closer to one indicates more balanced service. Table 2 reports the
tenth percentile of these ratios, using the same request pairs with defined ratios under all four methods. eFAIR
improves P10 of rij by up to 108.7%, with the largest gain over EcoInfer on H200. A separate comparison
with an earlier eFAIR policy uses identical requests and commitments: request-level P10 increases by 8.86%
on H20 and 4.89% on H200, while electricity increases by 0.77% and 0.13%. The appendix details how these
changes redistribute service from ordinary to higher entitlement requests. These comparisons show improved
concurrent balance and redistribution toward higher entitlements, alongside higher overall P10.

normalized throughput across arrival periods. For Property 3, service-electricity demand is the reference

5.4
Scheduling Efficiency and Robustness
RQ3 examines whether eFAIR responds promptly during serving and maintains normalized throughput when
output-length predictions are inaccurate.
Scheduling response time. eFAIR produces decisions with millisecond-scale average response while GPU
execution continues. We measure response from the time a scheduling event enters the CPU queue until the
resulting decision is available, including CPU processing and queueing during workload replay. Table 4 reports
mean responses of 1.823 ms over 803,000 invocations on H20 and 1.609 ms over 1,264,780 invocations on
H200. The scheduler supplies each subsequent batch’s configuration and electricity reservation before launch.
Scheduling updates thus overlap with already launched GPU work.

Robustness to output-length prediction errors. eFAIR maintains higher P10 than all three baselines
within the hourly commitment under the tested output-length errors. Following the prediction-based VTC
experiment, we compare true-length inputs ( b
Ni = Ni) with four controlled perturbations: multiplying each
length by a uniform draw from [0.8, 1.2] or [0.5, 1.5], or by a fixed factor of 0.8 or 1.2, then rounding to
tokens. These errors affect predicted completion times, per-request service-electricity demand, and online
standalone-throughput estimates. Actual requests, the fixed standalone throughputs Bi used to calculate
observed qH
i , the commitment, and its associated aggregate demand estimate remain unchanged. Relative
to true-length inputs, P10 decreases by at most 0.81% on H20 and 0.74% on H200; absolute consumption
deviations remain below 0.261% and 0.018%, respectively (Table 5). The resulting service gains therefore
persist across both random length errors and systematic overestimation or underestimation.

6
Conclusion
Fair LLM serving under hourly electricity commitments requires allocating both computing capacity among
concurrent requests and electricity across arrival times. We formulate this problem as leximin optimization of
throughput normalized by standalone throughput and service entitlement, subject to the hourly electricity
budget. eFAIR uses a common service target to coordinate request dispatching, electricity reservations, and
GPU frequency selection, directing available electricity toward requests with lower normalized throughput
while accounting for future demand. Across H20 and H200 configurations with 32 replicas, eFAIR improves
the tenth percentile of normalized throughput by 28.0%–31.0% over the best budget-feasible baseline, with
absolute consumption deviations below 0.26%. Additional results show more balanced normalized through-
put among concurrent requests, closer alignment between electricity allocation and service demand, and
robustness to the tested output-length errors.

A
Commitment Planning and Electricity Demand
The common target z connects the request throughput definition to both advance commitment planning
and retrospective demand evaluation. We first estimate the electricity required per request, then use these
estimates to construct the hourly commitment and the common demand profile. The final accounting rules
define the electricity available for online decisions.
Per-request electricity demand. We estimate the electricity needed to provide each request with normalized
throughput of at least z. For request i and a fixed candidate configuration c, let bTi(c) be the predicted average
output throughput and bEi(c) the incremental service electricity above the fixed operating floor. The estimate
is the minimum service electricity among candidate configurations that meet this target:
ei(z) =
min
c:
b
Ti(c)
wiBi ≥z
bEi(c).
(A.1)
Each estimate assumes that the request is served alone without queueing and includes prefill, decoding,
and the execution gaps represented in the profile. The target z, standalone throughput Bi, candidate
configurations, and profiled execution model are fixed before method comparison. If no configuration
meets the target, the target is recorded as infeasible for that request. Every request in the two evaluated
workloads has a feasible configuration. Applying the same rule to every method gives a common reference
demand that accounts for entitlement.
Hourly commitment planning. The commitment combines total expected service electricity with fixed
operating electricity. Let bDh denote the estimated sum of ei(z) used in commitment planning for the expected
hourly request and entitlement mix, and let ∆h be the hour duration. The commitment is
Ch = Pfloor∆h + bDh.
(A.2)
The evaluated conditions use z = 0.6 and an accurate aggregate service-demand estimate constructed from
the recorded request population. The eFAIR scheduler receives the aggregate estimate; individual requests
become visible upon arrival. H20 uses 7.468284 MJ of expected service electricity and 10.207262 MJ of fixed
costs; H200 uses 8.463753 MJ and 10.544268 MJ, respectively. The resulting commitment is fixed before
evaluating any serving policy.
Demand over time. The common demand profile distributes each request’s electricity estimate across the
time required to meet the target. For arrival time ai and total output count Ni, the target throughput zwiBi
gives the reference interval

(A.3)
For five-minute interval Ik, the demand is
Dk =

(A.4)
Here | · | denotes interval duration, so a request crossing a boundary contributes only its overlapping fraction.
Recorded arrivals and request attributes instantiate this fixed rule; the target interval Ji is identical across
methods for each request. All methods use the same Dk; reference demand beyond the hour is recorded
outside the displayed hourly shares. The calculation uses actual arrivals only after execution, while the online
scheduler uses the aggregate service-demand estimate associated with Ch.
Adjustable electricity. Subtracting fixed operating costs from actual consumption isolates electricity consumed
by serving work above the fixed operating floor. For actual interval electricity Ek and interval duration |Ik|,
Ak = Ek −Pfloor|Ik|.
(A.5)
The fixed operating power is the pool’s minimum GPU idle power plus the assumed scheduler operating power.
The scheduler power component is 500 W for eFAIR and 400 W for the baselines, while all methods use the
17


--- Page 18 ---
same absolute Ch. We retain total electricity Ek, demand Dk, and request backlog alongside the normalized
shares used by TV. This preserves the magnitude, timing, and shape of electricity expenditure.
Current budget and surplus. The ELECTRICITY BUDGET ALLOCATOR reserves electricity for expected future
requests before allocating the current budget. Let Dfuture be the estimated service demand of later arrivals
and Dactive the demand of unfinished work not already reserved for execution. For the unreserved electricity
Rh(t) defined in the main paper, the current budget is
A(t) = Rh(t) −max{Rh(t), 0}
Dfuture
Dfuture + Dactive
.
(A.6)
The reserved fraction is zero when the denominator is zero. The surplus S(t) is the positive part of Rh(t) −
Dfuture −Dactive. Running work has already been deducted from Rh(t) and from active uncommitted demand,
preventing a second reservation for the same running work. The current budget and surplus are shared across
all workers and updated after each reservation.
B
Evaluation Metrics and Aggregation
All metrics use the recorded request IDs, service entitlements, and standalone throughputs for the evalu-
ated workload. We define the observation window, identify concurrent requests, and specify how request
and pair measurements are aggregated.
Observation window. Every request arriving within the evaluated hour is included at the common endpoint.
For endpoint H = 3600 seconds and request arrival ai < H, let ni(H) be the produced output and define
τ H
i
=
(
ci −ai,
completed by H,
H −ai,
otherwise.
(B.1)
The request’s normalized throughput is qH
i
=
ni(H)
wiBiτ H
i , using the same full-request standalone throughput
Bi for all policies. Requests with no output receive zero normalized throughput, and service and electricity
accounting both end at H. This definition includes all observed output and elapsed waiting and execution
time.
Concurrent request pairs. The main comparison uses the same request pairs under all four methods.
Request i is outstanding on [ai, ai + τ H
i ). The requests in each pair must overlap for a positive duration
under every method; their ratios use hour-end normalized throughputs: rij =
min(qH
i ,qH
j )
max(qH
i ,qH
j ). If only one
request has zero normalized throughput, the ratio is zero; if both values are zero, the ratio is undefined.
Pairs undefined under any method are excluded from all columns, retaining 922,870 of 922,941 pairs
on H20 and 1,794,482 of 1,794,525 on H200. Supplementary comparisons use separate eFAIR–baseline
intersections with explicit undefined counts.
Pair-level and request-level statistics. Pair statistics give equal weight to concurrent pairs, while request
statistics give equal weight to requests. The main concurrent table takes the tenth percentile over defined pair
ratios. For the supplemental request summary, fi is the minimum defined rij among request i’s competitors,
and percentiles are then taken over requests with at least one defined competitor ratio. The global minimum
and requests without competitors are retained with the coverage counts. These aggregation rules distinguish
balance across concurrent pairs from each request’s least balanced comparison.
Percentiles and matched requests. Throughput percentiles and request-level comparisons give equal weight
to each request. For an ordered population of size n, quantiles use linear interpolation at zero-based index
(n −1)p for percentile fraction p. The baseline weak group contains exactly ⌈0.1n⌉requests, ranked by
baseline normalized throughput and then input order to resolve ties. The same IDs are compared under eFAIR,
counting higher, lower, and unchanged normalized throughput. Arrival plots use the same five-minute arrival
groups across methods; boxes report the 25th percentile, median, and 75th percentile, and whiskers retain
the actual minimum and maximum. These rules make all three types of service comparison reproducible.
18


--- Page 19 ---
C
Implementation and Measurement Details
This appendix describes the scheduler inputs and prediction procedures, the response-time and model
measurements, and the configurations used for baseline comparisons.
Scheduler inputs. The eFAIR scheduler receives the hourly commitment and the aggregate service-electricity
estimate used to set that commitment. Individual requests become visible upon arrival; future request at-
tributes and arrival times are not exposed. The H20 population contains 12,065 ordinary requests and 23,532
with entitlement 1.5; H200 contains 20,900 and 39,786, respectively. All methods and runs share these fixed
input conditions.
Completion-time prediction. Completion-time predictions combine the profiled execution model’s batch
estimates with the remaining prefill and decoding work. Predicted output length b
Ni and observed output
determine remaining decoding work. The fixed single-request reference profile sums per-output time costs
through b
Ni outputs to estimate standalone throughput bBi. Evaluation uses the fixed standalone throughput
Bi for the full request and the actual output length. For decoding-only batches, the prediction applies the
current batch’s slowdown to the profiled context-dependent costs and includes recent CPU decision time. For
supported ordinary-request prefill batches with completion predictions, frequency selection compares the
electricity required to complete service; for decoding-only batches, selection compares incremental iteration
electricity among candidates predicted to meet the target. For batches without a completion projection,
FREQUENCY SELECTOR selects the frequency with the shortest predicted iteration duration among those
whose predicted electricity fits the current shared budget. If none fits, FREQUENCY SELECTOR selects the
frequency with minimum predicted iteration electricity. Each decision reserves electricity for the next iteration;
subsequent decisions incorporate observed progress.
Output-length prediction errors. The study in Section 5.4 of the paper compares true-length inputs ( b
Ni = Ni)
with four controlled error conditions. The random conditions use one fixed seed (20261028), with a separate
multiplier for each request derived from the request ID. Predictions are rounded to the nearest positive token
count and bounded by the declared output and context limits; the public output cap is 8,192 for all requests
and is independent of their realized lengths. When an unfinished request reaches the predicted length, the
estimate doubles, subject to these same limits. Completion reveals the final output count and settles the
request’s reference work and arrived electricity demand. The predicted length is used to estimate completion
time, electricity demand, and standalone throughput. Evaluation always uses the original full-request stan-
dalone throughput, commitment, arrival sequence, and actual output lengths. The aggregate service-demand
estimate used to set Ch is held fixed to isolate per-request length uncertainty. Ten full-hour runs cover five
conditions on each hardware configuration, including matched true-length controls; each run uses a distinct
physical CPU core. Prediction errors, estimate extensions, and electricity deviations are archived.
Scheduling response-time measurement. The selected H20 run records 803,000 scheduler invocations and
790,499 serving iterations; H200 records 1,264,780 invocations and 1,242,954 iterations. Invocation counts
include calls that return without launching a batch. The scheduling queue records enqueue, processing-start,
and result-ready times. CPU processing duration is timed around each scheduler callback; queueing and
result-ready times follow the replay’s event scheduler. Mean response time is the sum of total queue wait and
total scheduler processing time, divided by the invocation count; both totals use this same population. On
H20, mean queueing and processing times are 1.132487 ms and 0.690336 ms, giving a mean response time of
1.822823 ms. On H200, they are 0.714393 ms and 0.895062 ms, giving a mean response time of 1.609455 ms.
The accumulated scheduler processing times, 554.34 and 1,132.06 seconds, exclude CPU queueing time.
Maximum recorded queue waits are 842.33 ms and 1,136.84 ms. The replay overlaps serving iterations
with scheduler processing; subsequent launches wait for the scheduling decision and the host/device launch
constraints. The reported implementation evaluates five frequency candidates sequentially. The evaluations
share dispatch, state-update, budget, and selection work. Parallel candidate evaluation retains this shared
work and adds task coordination.
Model calibration and validation. Hardware energy measurements use differences in NVML cumulative GPU
energy counters over each profiling window. The profiled execution model is checked against measurement
records that were available during model development but excluded from fitting the correction parameters.
19


--- Page 20 ---
H20 duration correction uses single-request decode at 1980 MHz: 9,254 steps in the first 60 seconds are
used to fit the correction, and 11,613 steps in the next 60 seconds are used to check it. The reported timing
error is
P
j |btj−tj|
P
j tj
, where tj is measured step duration. The timing error decreases from 2.6976% to 2.1759%;
signed total-duration bias decreases from −2.1549% to −0.0115%. For effective decode power, batch-size-one
windows are used to fit the correction and batch-size-two windows are used to check it at 345, 750, 1170,
1575, and 1980 MHz. Each check contains 128 target calls with contexts from 3,080 to 3,209 tokens; corrected
errors range from −0.033% to +0.980%. The duration check covers single-request decode at 1980 MHz, while
the power checks cover the five listed frequencies. The H200 power correction uses two disjoint intervals
on eight GPUs from one 90-second capture. Three separate saved measurement checks last 93.8, 101.0, and
305.7 seconds. The first two use two-request, 2,048-token-prompt configurations at 1575 and 750 MHz; the
third uses a Poisson arrival trace, mostly at 1170 MHz. Their aggregate energy errors are +2.22%, −0.88%,
and −2.94%. Counter sampling and window interpolation contribute uncertainty to these checks.
Worker assignment and batch selection. The REQUEST DISPATCHER first uses an idle worker for a higher
entitlement arrival; otherwise the dispatcher favors residents with the same entitlement, ready workers,
and smaller groups, followed by earlier completion among busy workers. Ordinary arrivals favor groups of
ordinary requests below the configured batch-size limit, using ready groups before waiting for a busy one.
Higher entitlement requests receive batch priority when every ordinary resident reaches both z and the median
normalized throughput of active higher entitlement requests with output; without that median, the threshold
is z. Before output begins, the resident request’s prediction uses elapsed time plus remaining service at the
estimated standalone throughput. The dispatcher uses an available idle worker when a destination resident
or the incoming request falls below the higher entitlement median; without that median the dispatcher retains
the preferred destination. The incoming request estimate includes the selected worker’s remaining execution
before admission. Token, sequence, and memory limits determine whether a batch is feasible.
Baseline configurations. The principal vLLM and Weighted VTC operating points are 1365 MHz for H20
and 1170 MHz for H200; their default points use 1980 and 1710 MHz, respectively. The same profiled VTC
service cost applies at both operating points. The H20 1365 MHz electricity and duration estimates use
interpolation between the profiled 1170 and 1575 MHz calibration points. Baseline frequencies are chosen
to make consumption as close as possible to the commitment without exceeding the budget or changing the
original scheduling policy.
D

policies are compared at the current commitment unless a different commitment is stated.

Leximin comparison. The empirical leximin comparison sorts normalized throughput for all 35,597 H20
requests or all 60,686 H200 requests, including zeros. The first six H20 values and first four H200 values tie
at zero across methods. At the next rank, eFAIR is positive while every baseline remains at zero, establishing
the ordering reported in the main paper. The remaining sorted values describe the breadth of the gains: on
H20, every sorted position through the lowest 10% is at least as high under eFAIR; on H200, values at ranks
6–115 are lower than those under vLLM, and values at ranks 48–77 are lower than those under Weighted VTC.
The P1 and P10 values complement these local differences with stronger lower-tail service at larger ranks.

Earlier commitments. Earlier experiments used different hourly commitments, so their P10 values correspond

conditions scaled from default vLLM consumption and their raw outcomes remain in the supplied archive.
